question: What drives the difference between how Schwab earns on client assets and how an advisor-led model earns?

claims.text: How it earns - Schwab: The 2025 10-K (published 2026-02-25) states that Schwab's largest sources of net revenues are net interest revenue, asset management and administration fees, trading revenue, and bank deposit account fees. Net interest revenue is the difference between interest generated on interest-earning assets and interest paid on funding sources. Schwab's primary funding source is uninvested client cash held on its balance sheet.

How it earns - Schwab: The 2025 10-K describes bank deposit account fees as revenue from sweeping uninvested client cash off-balance sheet to accounts at the TD Depository Institutions. Schwab provides marketing, recordkeeping and support services in exchange. The revenues are based on floating and fixed yields elected by the Company, less interest paid to clients and other fees.

How it earns - Schwab: In its 1Q26 10-Q (published 2026-05-08), Schwab says it sets the rates paid on certain brokerage client cash balances and bank deposits and the rates charged on certain margin and bank loans. It also controls the composition of its investment securities. It says this lets it take actions to manage its net interest spread, depending on competitive factors and market conditions.

How it earns - Schwab: The 1Q26 10-Q (published 2026-05-08) says Schwab earns mutual fund and ETF service fees and asset management fees based on daily balances of certain client assets. Changes in equity valuations therefore directly affect fee revenue.

How it earns - Schwab: In its 2Q26 results release (published 2026-07-21), Schwab reported net interest margin of 3.00% and client transactional sweep cash of $485.7 billion. Asset management and administration fees grew 16% year-over-year to $1.8 billion. Trading revenue was $1.2 billion, up 28% year-over-year.

How it earns - Schwab: In its 3Q26 results release (published 2026-10-15), Schwab reported net interest margin of 3.04% and client transactional sweep cash of $492.8 billion. Asset management and administration fees grew 14% year-over-year to $1.9 billion. Trading revenue was $1.2 billion, up 16% year-over-year.

How it earns - Morgan Stanley: The 2025 10-K (published 2026-02-19) says Wealth Management asset management revenues relate to advisory services on fee-based assets, account service and administration, and distribution of products. They are generally based on the net asset value of the account in which a client is invested.

How it earns - Morgan Stanley: On the 2Q26 call (published 2026-07-15), the CFO cited Wealth Management asset management revenues of $5.3 billion and transactional revenues of $1.2 billion. She said deposits grew sequentially to $436 billion and net interest income increased to $2.3 billion. She said NII outperformed on higher-than-expected sweep balances and strong loan growth.

How it earns - Edward Jones: The 2025 10-K (published 2026-03-13) shows 2025 total revenue of $17,897 million. Asset-based fees were $14,138 million (79%), account and activity fees $747 million (4%), trade revenue $1,832 million (10%), interest and dividends $1,062 million (6%), and other revenue, net $118 million (1%). Asset-based fees include advisory programs fees, service fees and other asset-based fees.

How it earns - Edward Jones: The 1Q26 10-Q (published 2026-05-07) says advisory program fees are based on the average daily market value of client assets in the program. Trade revenue is commissions and principal transactions. Net interest and dividends revenue is a separate category.

How it earns - Merrill: The 2Q26 10-Q (published 2026-07-31) says Merrill Wealth Management revenue of $5.7 billion increased 16 percent. It attributes this primarily to higher asset management fees (higher market valuations and positive AUM flows) and higher brokerage fees from increased transactional volume.

How it earns - Raymond James: The FY2025 10-K (published 2025-11-25) says the Private Client Group generally charges either asset-based fees or sales commissions. It also earns servicing fees from product companies and from banks to which it sweeps client cash through RJBDP, its multi-bank sweep program.

How it earns - Raymond James: The fiscal 3Q26 release (published 2026-07-22) says PCG asset management and related administrative fees grew 19% to $1.73 billion, mainly on market appreciation and net inflows into fee-based accounts. Pre-tax income was affected by lower interest rates. Total clients' domestic cash sweep and Enhanced Savings Program balances were $58.8 billion.

What drives it - Schwab: The 2025 10-K (published 2026-02-25) says a reduction in clients' allocation to cash, a change in how that cash is allocated, or a transfer of cash away would likely reduce its income. It cites 2022-2023, when clients moved from sweep cash into higher-yielding alternatives at Schwab and Schwab used higher-cost funding that hurt net income.

What drives it - Schwab: The 2Q26 10-Q (published 2026-08-07) says Schwab establishes the rates paid on client-related liabilities. Management expects it will generally adjust those rates at some fraction of any movement in short-term rates.

What drives it - Schwab: The 2025 10-K says Schwab monitors its pricing against competitors and periodically adjusts deposit and loan rates, advisory fees, fund expense ratios and trade commission rates. It says price competition such as reduced commissions or higher deposit rates could affect results.

What drives it - Schwab: On the 2Q26 call (published 2026-07-21), the CEO said just 5% of Schwab retail households are in a fee-based advice solution. He said clients in Schwab Wealth Advisory generate 3x the ROCA of retail clients. He framed the combination as a way to "diversify our economics over the long term."

What drives it - Schwab: On the 1Q26 call (published 2026-04-16), the CEO said Schwab does not currently see sweep-cash monetization as a big risk. He said clients have intentionally allocated their cash and Schwab makes it easy for them to land in the right cash solution.

What drives it - Morgan Stanley: On the 4Q25 call (published 2026-01-15), a company representative named two drivers of expanded margins: building out fee-based revenues and fee-based assets, and technology-driven efficiency. The representative also cited investment in self-directed (E*TRADE) activity.

What drives it - Morgan Stanley: The 1Q26 supplement (published 2026-04-15) shows Wealth Management deposits of $419 billion with an annualized weighted average cost of deposits of 2.51% at period end and 2.53% on a period-average basis. Fee-based client assets were $2,792 billion, 48% of advisor-led client assets.

What drives it - Edward Jones: The 2025 10-K (published 2026-03-13) says revenue growth came primarily from asset-based fees, driven by growth in advisory programs, higher average market levels and more client dollars invested in advisory programs. Interest and dividends revenue decreased on lower interest rates.

What drives it - Edward Jones: The 2025 10-K risk factors say lower interest rates negatively affect revenue from certain cash solutions products. They say the firm has waived certain fees in low-rate environments to maintain a positive client yield, and that this could happen again.

What drives it - Merrill: The 1Q26 10-Q (published 2026-05-01) says Merrill Wealth Management revenue of $5.6 billion increased 11 percent, driven by higher asset management fees and higher brokerage fees. This was partially offset by the impact of lower AUM pricing.

What drives it - Raymond James: The FY2025 10-K (published 2025-11-25) says PCG results are affected by the level of client cash and by its allocation among RJBDP, the Client Interest Program (CIP) and the Enhanced Savings Program (ESP). The PCG segment may earn different amounts from each destination.

What drives it - Raymond James: The FY2025 10-K says RJBDP fees from banks generally fluctuate with average program balances and the level of short-term interest rates. The 2Q26 10-Q (published 2026-08-05) says PCG earns servicing fees for administrative services on swept deposits. These fees vary with client cash balances, short-term rates and interest paid to clients.

What drives it - Raymond James: On the fiscal 2Q26 call (published 2026-04-22), the CEO said industry transactional or sweep cash balances have gone down 40% to 50%. He said the average cash balance per fee-based account is now less than $10,000. He said the firm feels sweep balances have stabilized.

adjacent.text: Merrill-related: On the 2Q25 call (published 2025-07-16), the CFO described GWIM as primarily a fee-based, advice-driven model. He said about 30% of revenue is net interest income from GWIM clients and their loan and deposit balances. GWIM covers Merrill and the Private Bank.
adjacent.differs_because: GWIM includes both Merrill and Bank of America Private Bank; the two have different reporting scopes, so GWIM figures are not Merrill's.

adjacent.text: Merrill-related: The 2Q26 GWIM deck (published 2026-07-14) shows an average deposit rate paid of 2.02% and average loans and leases of $270.3 billion. Average deposits were $281.6 billion.
adjacent.differs_because: GWIM includes both Merrill and Bank of America Private Bank; the two have different reporting scopes, so GWIM figures are not Merrill's.

adjacent.text: Merrill-related: The 2Q26 10-Q (published 2026-07-31) says GWIM noninterest expense rose primarily on higher revenue-related incentives. It also says brokerage deposits declined as clients moved balances to higher-yielding cash alternatives.
adjacent.differs_because: GWIM includes both Merrill and Bank of America Private Bank; the two have different reporting scopes, so GWIM figures are not Merrill's.

adjacent.text: A trade report (published 2026-09-29) says Merrill's full-service brokers face a minimum transaction commission of $75 or $0.04 per share, capped at 5.00% of principal trade value. It says fee-based programs are typically 1.00% to 1.40% of assets, and as high as 1.75% per sources.
adjacent.differs_because: Trade-press reporting is indicative, not authoritative.

adjacent.text: A trade report (published 2026-09-30) cites Fitch as identifying Schwab as having the largest absolute earnings exposure to client cash. It says Schwab generated nearly $3.4 billion in net interest revenue in Q2 2026, largely on approximately $485.7 billion in sweep accounts. It also says higher deposit costs and cash sorting can erode the earnings benefit.
adjacent.differs_because: Trade-press reporting is indicative, not authoritative.

adjacent.text: Edward Jones: The 2025 10-K (published 2026-03-13) says financial advisor compensation and benefits increased 12% to $6,778 million, primarily due to increases in revenues on which commissions are earned. Variable compensation rose 11% to $2,652 million.
adjacent.differs_because: Aggregate compensation expense covers all employees and pay types; it is not the advisor payout grid.

adjacent.text: Raymond James: The 2Q25 10-Q (published 2025-08-06) says compensation-related expenses increased $484 million, or 10%, primarily on higher commission expense from higher compensable revenues, including asset management and related administrative fees and brokerage revenues.
adjacent.differs_because: Aggregate compensation expense covers all employees and pay types; it is not the advisor payout grid.

adjacent.text: Morgan Stanley (firm-wide): The 2Q26 release (published 2026-07-15) shows firm-wide compensation expense of $8,187 million against net revenues of $21,348 million.
adjacent.differs_because: Aggregate compensation expense covers all employees and pay types; it is not the advisor payout grid.
